records.sourceFile: Effect of Social Media on Diet, Lifestyle, and Performance of Athletes - A Review of Current Evidence.pdf

paper.citation: Nath S, Bhattacharya S, Golla VB, Kumar R. Effect of Social Media on Diet, Lifestyle, and Performance of Athletes: A Review of Current Evidence. Current Nutrition Reports. 2024.
paper.abstract: This review searched PubMed, Embase and Google Scholar and retained 22 articles on how social media influences the diet, lifestyle and performance practices of athletes. The authors describe social media as a powerful, but credibility-limited, source of nutrition and lifestyle advice, with links to supplement choices, dietary trends and body image concerns. They conclude that social media advice should be used with caution and checked against sports nutrition and coaching advice.
paper.tldr: This review of 22 articles found that athletes often use social media for diet and supplement advice, and that the credibility of that advice is hard to judge. Trending foods and supplements should be checked with a sports dietitian and coach before use.
paper.methods: Literature was searched in PubMed, Embase and Google Scholar using combined keywords for social media, athletes, diet, nutrition, lifestyle and athletic performance. The initial search returned 121 records, 102 after removing duplicates; titles and abstracts were screened, and 22 articles were retained after full-text review by at least three authors. The paper describes no formal quality appraisal of the included studies.
paper.findings: Included studies report high social media use for nutrition information among athletes, for example 65% of 306 New Zealand athletes used it for nutrition needs in the past year, and 64% of 455 athletes in Lebanon relied on online social media for supplement information. Several studies link fitspiration and thinspiration content to body image concerns, mainly in non-athlete samples. The authors note that literature on social media effects on athlete lifestyle and performance is scarce, that a cited systematic review rated evidence for health behavior change interventions delivered through online social networks as modest, and that social-media-delivered dietary weight loss interventions were not consistently effective.
paper.limitations: The search was limited to three databases and English-language journal articles, and no risk-of-bias or quality appraisal is reported. The included set mixes original research with viewpoints and commentaries, many studies are cross-sectional or qualitative, and several sampled non-athletes such as gym users, military personnel or young adults. The review does not pool or quantify effects, so the strength of its conclusions cannot be graded.
paper.practicalImplications: Ask athletes which diet, supplement and lifestyle trends they follow online, and have those trends checked with a sports dietitian and coach before use. For supplements, check for doping risk, since the review cites evidence that some products contain doping substances. Watch for body image concerns in athletes who follow image-focused fitness or diet content, which the review links to disordered eating.
paper.athleteDev: The review gives performance staff a reason to ask athletes where they get nutrition and supplement advice, and to route trending diet or supplement ideas through a sports dietitian. It contains no measured performance outcomes, so it cannot guide training or performance programming.
paper.rtp: The review does not study return to sport or recovery from injury, so it cannot show whether social media nutrition advice helps or harms recovery. It supports only the general advice to verify online recovery-nutrition claims with a qualified sports dietitian.

records.sourceFile: Effect of personalized sodium replacement on fluid and sodium balance and thermophysiological strain during and after ultraendurance running in the heat.pdf

paper.citation: McCubbin AJ, da Costa RJS. Effect of Personalized Sodium Replacement on Fluid and Sodium Balance and Thermophysiological Strain During and After Ultraendurance Running in the Heat. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2023.
paper.abstract: Nine ultraendurance runners completed two 5-hour treadmill runs in 30 C heat in a double-blind randomized crossover design, receiving sodium capsules that replaced 100% of their estimated sweat sodium losses or placebo. Sodium replacement did not change ad libitum fluid intake or heat strain during exercise, but it raised plasma sodium more than placebo. Over the next 24 hours, fluid intake and urinary sodium excretion were higher after sodium replacement, and the authors conclude that personalized replacement was not needed to limit body-water loss.
paper.tldr: In 9 ultraendurance runners exercising 5 hours in 30 C heat, sodium capsules matched to sweat sodium losses did not change drinking or heat strain during exercise, but raised plasma sodium. Over the next day they increased fluid intake and reduced sodium conservation by the kidneys, so the effect on hydration needs careful reading.
paper.methods: Double-blind randomized crossover trial. Nine runners (7 men, 2 women) completed two 5-hour runs at 60% VO2max in a 30 C climate chamber. Sodium chloride capsules replaced 100% of sweat sodium losses estimated from a familiarization run, or matched maltodextrin capsules were given as placebo; a fixed carbohydrate solution and ad libitum water were provided. Plasma sodium and osmolality, plasma volume, heart rate, rectal temperature, thermal comfort, and 24-hour fluid and urine measures were collected.
paper.findings: Ad libitum water intake during exercise did not differ between trials (1,553 vs 1,216 mL; P = .07), nor did net water balance, heart rate, rectal temperature or perceived exertion. Plasma sodium rose more with sodium replacement at 2.5 and 5 hours (for example 4 vs 1 mmol/L at 2.5 hours), and postexercise urinary sodium was higher (66 vs 21 mmol). After exercise, total fluid intake (2,541 vs 1,998 mL, P = .04) and net water balance (+1,532 vs +774 mL, P < .01) were higher with sodium, giving a total net water balance across exercise and the 24-hour recovery of +265 vs -812 mL (P < .01); net sodium balance at 24 hours was positive with sodium and negative with placebo.
paper.limitations: The sample was 9 runners (7 men and 2 women), one 5-hour session at one intensity, so the findings do not cover longer events, cooler conditions or sex-specific effects. Sweat sodium was estimated from one familiarization run and replacement ranged from 78% to 231% of actual losses, and sodium was given as capsules rather than in drinks. The authors conclude that sodium replacement did not substantially affect overall body-water balance, but Table 2 shows a significant difference in postexercise and total water balance, and the abstract labels postexercise total fluid intake as ad libitum intake.
paper.practicalImplications: In about 5 hours of heat running, replacing estimated sweat sodium did not significantly change drinking during exercise in this small sample. Sweat sodium estimates varied between sessions, so an individual sodium plan should not be treated as precise. Over the next 24 hours, the sodium trial had higher total fluid intake and better water balance, so staff should not read this trial as showing that sodium is unneeded for hydration.
paper.athleteDev: The trial measured hydration, plasma sodium and heat strain rather than running performance. Heart rate, rectal temperature and perceived exertion did not differ with sodium replacement over 5 hours, which suggests little effect on heat strain during a single run in these runners.
paper.rtp: The trial used healthy runners and does not study injury, illness or heat-related injury recovery. It cannot inform return-to-sport timing or readiness after an injury or heat illness.

records.sourceFile: Effects of Different Vitamin-C Enriched Collagen Derivatives on Collagen Synthesis.pdf

paper.citation: Lis DM, Baar K. Effects of Different Vitamin-C Enriched Collagen Derivatives on Collagen Synthesis. International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism. 2019 (accepted manuscript).
paper.abstract: Randomized double-blind crossover in 10 recreationally active men comparing placebo, vitamin C-enriched gelatin, hydrolyzed collagen, and a gummy, each taken before 6 min of jump rope. Amino acid levels rose similarly for all supplements, and PINP changes were positive for gelatin and hydrolyzed collagen, but no change reached statistical significance because of large variability.
paper.tldr: A single 15 g dose of gelatin or hydrolyzed collagen taken before a short jump-rope bout did not produce a statistically significant rise in the bone collagen marker PINP. The study is too small and too affected by assay problems to show a real effect on collagen synthesis.
paper.methods: Randomized, double-blind, crossover trial with four trials at least 48 h apart: maltodextrin placebo, 15 g gelatin, 15 g hydrolyzed collagen, or a gummy with about 7.5 g each of gelatin and collagen, all with blackcurrant cordial. Participants jumped rope for 6 min one hour after ingestion; serum PINP was measured by ELISA at baseline and 4 h, and a subgroup of four men had serum amino acids measured at 1 h.
paper.findings: Mean PINP change from baseline at 4 h was 20.4% (± 52.9) for gelatin, 19.6% (± 47.5) for hydrolyzed collagen, -23.8% (± 30.5) for the gummy, and -6.8% (± 43.7) for placebo, none statistically significant (P > 0.05); the methods state data are mean ± SEM. In the four-man subgroup, serum glycine, lysine, proline, hydroxyproline and hydroxylysine rose at 1 h to a similar extent across the three collagen products, while leucine did not change.
paper.limitations: The sample was ten men, five outlying PINP values were removed, and the amino acid arm had only four men. The authors report that vitamin C inhibits the PINP ELISA and that serum clotting time may have affected results, so the PINP data are weak. The text and Figure 2 caption describe increases and a 'strong trend' for gelatin, but the Results report no significant change; the Results are reported here.
paper.practicalImplications: This study does not support using gelatin or hydrolyzed collagen to speed tendon or bone collagen synthesis after exercise. Staff could treat the 1-hour amino acid response as confirmation that the products are absorbed similarly, but that is not a training outcome. The authors suggest vitamin C co-ingestion may matter for the collagen response, which has not been tested.
paper.athleteDev: This study measured no performance or tissue outcome, so it gives no evidence of a performance or tissue-strength benefit from gelatin or collagen before loading. Its only usable finding for staff is that the products raised circulating amino acids similarly, which does not show a training effect.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It tested recreationally active men after one 6-minute jump-rope session and measured no injured, rehabilitating, or tissue-load outcomes.

records.sourceFile: Effects of an individualized vs standardized Vitamin D supplementation on the 24(OH)D level in athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Tuma C, Schick A, Pommerening N, Braun H, Thevis M. Effects of an Individualized vs. Standardized Vitamin D Supplementation on the 25(OH)D Level in Athletes. Nutrients. 2023;15:4747.
paper.abstract: Vitamin D is important for athletes, and a 25(OH)D target of at least 40 ng/mL is often suggested. In a 10-week winter study in Germany, athletes with insufficient vitamin D were randomized to an individualized loading dose, a standard 2000 IU daily dose or no supplement. The authors report that the individualized group had higher 25(OH)D on its calculated target day than the standard group at 5 weeks (41.1 vs 32.5 ng/mL).
paper.tldr: In winter, an individualized vitamin D loading dose gave higher 25(OH)D on its calculated target day than a standard 2000 IU daily dose at 5 weeks. By 10 weeks both groups had similar levels, and only 30% of the individualized group were at or above 40 ng/mL.
paper.methods: Ninety athletes training at least 5 hours per week were enrolled in Germany from January to April. Athletes with 25(OH)D below 30 ng/mL were matched on baseline level and randomized to an individualized group (4000 IU per day until a calculated target day, from the Groningen formula, then 1000 IU per day), a standard group (2000 IU per day) or a control group with no supplement. Sufficient athletes were monitored without supplementation. Total 25(OH)D was measured from capillary VAMS samples at baseline, at a second time point and at 10 weeks, and a vitamin D questionnaire was completed.
paper.findings: At the second measurement, the individualized group had 41.1 plus or minus 10.9 ng/mL at its calculated time (41 plus or minus 12 days), compared with 32.5 plus or minus 6.4 ng/mL in the standard group at 5 weeks (P < 0.001). At the final measurement the individualized and standard groups had similar means (37.9 plus or minus 10.3 vs 38.1 plus or minus 6.8 ng/mL); the individualized group declined by 3.2 ng/mL on the 1000 IU maintenance dose while the standard group kept rising. The unsupplemented control group fell from 21.9 to 18.1 ng/mL and the sufficient group fell by 8.7 ng/mL. Half of the individualized group reached 40 ng/mL at the calculated day and 30% did so at the end, compared with 17% and 38% of the standard group at 5 and 10 weeks, and baseline 25(OH)D correlated negatively with the rise over the study (r = -0.54, P < 0.001).
paper.limitations: The abstract says all 90 athletes were insufficient and randomized, but only the 67 with levels below 30 ng/mL were randomized (28 INDV, 26 STAD, 13 CON), and the 23 sufficient athletes were monitored only. The key comparison used different time points (about 41 days for INDV versus 5 weeks for STAD), and final samples were taken at 77 and 78 days in the two supplemented groups rather than at 10 weeks. The reported weight difference between INDV athletes who did and did not reach 40 ng/mL has a 95% CI that includes zero (-0.21 to 18.66) yet is reported as P < 0.05; the abstract also says dried blood spots, while the Methods used VAMS whole-blood samples.
paper.practicalImplications: Athletes with low winter vitamin D may need more than 1000 IU daily to hold a level near 40 ng/mL, so periodic measurement during the season is sensible. The study does not show that individualized loading gives better levels than a standard dose by the end of 10 weeks.
paper.athleteDev: The study measured vitamin D status, not performance, and did not test jump, strength or endurance. Use it to guide winter vitamin D testing and supplementation, not as evidence that supplementation improves athletic performance.
paper.rtp: The study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It enrolled healthy athletes with low vitamin D and did not study injury, stress fractures or rehabilitation outcomes.

records.sourceFile: Effects of melatonin ingestion on physical performance and biochemical responses following exhaustive running exercise in soccer players.pdf

paper.citation: Farjallah MA, Graja A, Ben Mahmoud L, Ghattassi K, Boudaya M, Driss T, et al. Effects of melatonin ingestion on physical performance and biochemical responses following exhaustive running exercise in soccer players. Biology of Sport. 2022;39(2):473-479.
paper.abstract: In a double-blind randomized study, 13 professional soccer players ran to exhaustion at 100% of maximal aerobic speed after either 6 mg melatonin or placebo. Melatonin attenuated the post-exercise rise in malondialdehyde and the rise in creatine kinase and lactate dehydrogenase, but physical performance was not affected.
paper.tldr: In 13 professional soccer players, 6 mg melatonin before a running test to exhaustion did not change running time, but it blunted the rise in muscle-damage and lipid-peroxidation markers. These are acute, single-session findings and do not show a performance benefit.
paper.methods: Thirteen players completed three sessions at least 48 hours apart: anthropometrics and a maximal aerobic speed field test, then a crossover comparison of 6 mg melatonin or lactose placebo, each followed by a running test at 100% of maximal aerobic speed until exhaustion. Blood was sampled at rest and 3 minutes after the test for oxidative stress, antioxidant and muscle-damage markers, and oral temperature and a vigilance test were also recorded.
paper.findings: Physical performance did not differ between placebo (362.5 +/- 42.1 s) and melatonin (374.5 +/- 58.0 s; p = 0.19), nor did HR max or RPE. After the test, MDA rose only under placebo (1.55 to 2.89 umol/L), CK rose only under placebo, and post-exercise CK (310 vs 250 IU/L; p < 0.001) and LDH (272 vs 238 IU/L; p < 0.05) were lower after melatonin than placebo. SOD fell after the test in both conditions, GPx fell and uric acid and bilirubin rose only under placebo, and post-exercise oral temperature was lower after melatonin.
paper.limitations: Thirteen players, one 6 mg dose given in the afternoon, and only a 3-minute post-exercise blood sample, so delayed biochemical responses were not measured. The sex of the sample is not stated. The Abstract says melatonin alleviated changes in uric acid and total bilirubin, but the condition by exercise interaction for both was not significant (p > 0.05); only within-condition post hoc changes differed.
paper.practicalImplications: A single 6 mg afternoon dose did not improve running time to exhaustion in this group, so it should not be used for performance. Lower post-exercise muscle-damage markers suggest a possible recovery effect that needs testing over several days before staff act on it.
paper.athleteDev: Melatonin did not change running time to exhaustion in this study, so it cannot be recommended to improve performance. The lower CK, LDH and MDA after one session are an acute finding and need multi-day replication.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It used healthy players without injury and measured no injury, rehabilitation or return-to-play outcome.

records.sourceFile: Effects of pre-sleep protein consumption on muscle-related outcomes - A systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: Reis CEG, Loureiro LMR, Roschel H, da Costa THM. Effects of pre-sleep protein consumption on muscle-related outcomes - a systematic review. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. 2020.
paper.abstract: Nine clinical trials were reviewed for the acute effects of pre-sleep protein on overnight muscle protein synthesis and the chronic effects on muscle mass and strength. Roughly 20 to 40 g of casein about 30 minutes before sleep raised overnight protein synthesis, and pre-sleep protein augmented resistance-training gains in young but not older men, with the caveat that protein intake was often unmatched.
paper.tldr: In healthy adults, about 20 to 40 g of casein before sleep raised overnight muscle protein synthesis. Evidence that it adds to muscle size or strength over 10 to 12 weeks is limited, mostly to one young-men trial in which total protein intake was not matched.
paper.methods: Systematic search of PubMed, ScienceDirect and Web of Science (December 2019, updated June 2020) following PRISMA, with two independent screeners and a third author for disagreements. Eligible studies were human clinical trials in apparently healthy adults or older adults comparing pre-sleep protein with placebo, carbohydrate or water, reporting overnight muscle protein synthesis or chronic changes in muscle mass or strength. Data were summarized in tables, with protein synthesis rates converted to common units; no pooled meta-analysis was performed.
paper.findings: Acute: casein raised whole-body protein synthesis overnight in young men after evening resistance exercise (for example 41.5 vs 32.8 umol/kg/h in Res et al., p < 0.01) and in older men without exercise (Groen et al. +47.6%, p < 0.01; Kouw et al. +18.9%, p < 0.05). Fractional synthesis rose in both older-men studies but in only one of three young-men studies (Res et al., p = 0.05). Chronic: in young men on 12 weeks of resistance training, pre-sleep protein produced larger changes in quadriceps cross-sectional area (8.4 vs 4.8 cm2, p < 0.05), type II fiber area and strength (164 vs 130 kg, p < 0.01), but protein intake was about 1.9 vs 1.3 g/kg/day; with endurance training one study found greater whole-body lean mass gain (1.5 vs 0.4 kg, p < 0.01) and another no difference (p = 0.43), and in older men on resistance training muscle outcomes did not differ.
paper.limitations: Nine trials with small samples, and the chronic trials did not match total daily protein between groups, so timing cannot be separated from total intake. The Abstract and Conclusions say pre-sleep protein improves protein synthesis, while the Discussion warns that these acute tracer measures may not translate to muscle mass. The review has no pooled estimate, the search used three databases with keyword terms only, and two of the chronic trials are endurance training studies rather than resistance training.
paper.practicalImplications: A pre-sleep casein dose of about 20 to 40 g is supported for raising overnight protein synthesis in young adults after evening resistance exercise. Staff should present it as a way to raise total daily protein, because the chronic gains come from one trial in which the protein group also ate more protein overall.
paper.athleteDev: Pre-sleep casein increased overnight muscle protein synthesis after evening resistance exercise in young men, but chronic muscle and strength gains rest on one trial with unmatched protein intake. The outcomes were muscle size and strength rather than sport performance.
paper.rtp: This review does not inform return-to-sport decisions because it included apparently healthy or older adults and no injured participants or rehabilitation outcomes.

records.sourceFile: Equivalent Hypertrophy and Strength Gains in A-Hydroxy-A-Methylbutyrate- or Leucine-supplemented Men.pdf

paper.citation: Jakubowski JS, Wong EPT, Nunes EA, et al. Equivalent Hypertrophy and Strength Gains in A-Hydroxy-A-Methylbutyrate- or Leucine-supplemented Men. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2019;51(1):65-74.
paper.abstract: This randomized, double-blind trial compared whey protein with HMB-calcium against whey protein with leucine during 12 weeks of periodized resistance training in young men. Both groups gained fat- and bone-free mass, muscle size, strength and power, and the authors found no differences between the two supplements. The authors conclude that HMB added to whey was no more effective than leucine added to whey.
paper.tldr: In recreationally trained young men on a 12-week periodized program, whey with HMB produced the same gains in lean mass, muscle size, strength and power as whey with leucine. HMB does not add to a leucine-containing protein supplement in this setting.
paper.methods: Thirty recreationally trained men were recruited and 26 completed the trial (one injured in training, one injured outside the study, one relocated, one non-adherent). Participants took twice-daily whey protein (25 g) plus 1.5 g HMB-calcium or whey protein plus 1.5 g leucine during an 8-week periodized phase, a 2-week overreaching phase and a 2-week taper. Outcomes were DXA fat- and bone-free mass, ultrasound muscle thickness and cross-sectional area, muscle fiber size, 1-RM strength, Wingate and Optojump power, blood hormones and creatine kinase.
paper.findings: Fat- and bone-free mass rose in both groups (2.3 +/- 1.2 kg with HMB, 2.6 +/- 1.9 kg with leucine; P = 0.59), and muscle thickness (5% each) and cross-sectional area (2.2 vs 2.3 cm2) increased by similar amounts. Total 1-RM strength increased by 70 +/- 21 kg with HMB and 80 +/- 40 kg with leucine (P = 0.41), and peak Wingate power rose in both groups with no between-group difference (P = 0.39). Hormones and CK did not differ between groups at any phase. During overreaching (weeks 8 to 10), peak power fell by 39 +/- 74 W with HMB versus a change of 18 +/- 51 W with leucine, a significant group-by-time interaction (P = 0.03) that the abstract does not report.
paper.limitations: There was no non-supplemented control group, and HMB dosing and timing differed slightly from the recommended 1 g three times daily before exercise. The abstract states no group differences in mass and strength but omits the larger peak-power decline with HMB during overreaching (P = 0.03) reported in the results. Figure 2 lists 12 leucine participants for muscle thickness while the methods report 13 per group, and the authors could not explain why their fat-free mass gains were 3 to 3.7 times smaller than earlier HMB trials using the same program.
paper.practicalImplications: For resistance-trained young men who already take whey protein, this trial gives no reason to add HMB in place of leucine for muscle or strength gains over 12 weeks. The study does not test HMB against no supplement, so it cannot show whether HMB has any benefit on its own.
paper.athleteDev: Within a periodized program with adequate protein, HMB-calcium added to whey gave no greater gains in lean mass, muscle size, strength or power than leucine added to whey in trained non-athlete men. The single group-by-time difference, a larger peak-power decline with HMB during overreaching, comes from one small trial and needs confirmation before it informs load planning.
paper.rtp: Not applicable to return to sport. The trial enrolled healthy recreational exercisers, so it cannot inform rehabilitation, return-to-play or load-progression decisions after injury.

records.sourceFile: Ergogenic and Physiological Effects of Sports Supplements - Implications for Advertising and Consumer Information.pdf

paper.citation: Estevan Navarro P, González-Díaz C, García Pérez R, Gil-Izquierdo A, García CJ, Giménez-Monzo D, et al. Ergogenic and Physiological Effects of Sports Supplements: Implications for Advertising and Consumer Information. Nutrients. 2025;17:2706.
paper.abstract: This review summarizes the ergogenic and physiological effects of six Australian Institute of Sport category A sports supplements, drawing on position statements and systematic reviews with meta-analyses. It also examines how these supplements are regulated and marketed in Europe. The authors conclude that the evidence is strong for several supplements, that only caffeine and creatine have authorized health claims, and that regulation and labeling need updating.
paper.tldr: Caffeine, creatine, beta-alanine, nitrates, sodium bicarbonate and glycerol have dose and protocol patterns that expert bodies largely agree on. Only caffeine and creatine have EFSA-authorized health claims, so marketing for the others should be checked against the evidence. Use the dose tables as reference points, adjusted for the athlete and event.
paper.methods: The authors compiled sport, protocol, dose and reported effects for six AIS category A supplements from position or consensus statements (from 2015 onward) and systematic reviews with meta-analyses found with a PubMed keyword search and meta-analysis filter, prioritizing those from the last 2 years. Two reviewers extracted data independently with a predefined template, and a third resolved disagreements. The authors call it a narrative review that did not follow PRISMA or register a protocol.
paper.findings: Caffeine (3-6 mg/kg, about 60 minutes before exercise) and creatine (loading of 20-30 g/day or 0.3 g/kg for 5-7 days, or maintenance of 3-5 g/day) are the only supplements with EFSA-authorized health claims. Beta-alanine, nitrates and sodium bicarbonate are described as having evidence-supported ergogenic effects, while glycerol has shown mixed results. Citing earlier label analyses rather than new data, the authors report that only 2.78% of caffeine products fully complied with EFSA criteria and that only 25% of products analyzed partially or fully complied.
paper.limitations: The authors note that the work was not a formal systematic review, that secondary sources can carry publication bias and overrepresent male athletes, and that inter-individual response is not captured. The abstract describes the effects as supported by strong evidence, while the limitations call some effects, such as those of beta-alanine and glycerol, modest and context-dependent. The regulatory analysis covers only Europe, the product-compliance figures come from cited prior studies, and AIS category B supplements are excluded.
paper.practicalImplications: Use the protocol and dose tables as starting references when advising on the six supplements, adjusting for the athlete, event and conditions the authors name. Check any product claim against the authorized EFSA claims, since only caffeine and creatine have them. The authors' labeling and advertising recommendations are proposals and are not established requirements.
paper.athleteDev: The review summarizes doses, timing and sport contexts for caffeine, creatine, beta-alanine, nitrates, sodium bicarbonate and glycerol. It notes that caffeine response depends on individual factors, such as CYP1A2 genotype and time of day, and that sodium bicarbonate has gastrointestinal side effects. The effects of individual supplements in a specific sport still need to be confirmed with trials in that context.
paper.rtp: Not applicable to return to sport. The review covers performance and recovery effects in athletes and does not study injured athletes or rehabilitation.

records.sourceFile: Evaluating the effects of increased protein intake on muscle strength, hypertrophy and power adaptations with concurrent training - A narrative review.pdf

paper.citation: Camera DM. Evaluating the Effects of Increased Protein Intake on Muscle Strength, Hypertrophy and Power Adaptations with Concurrent Training: A Narrative Review. Sports Medicine. 2021.
paper.abstract: Narrative review of protein intake during concurrent resistance and aerobic training, covering muscle protein synthesis, lean mass, strength, and muscle damage and power outcomes.
paper.tldr: Protein above standard intakes raises muscle protein synthesis after a single concurrent session and may add lean mass over long programs. It does not appear to restore the strength or power lost to concurrent training.
paper.methods: Narrative review of acute and chronic studies, organized by outcome: muscle protein synthesis, lean mass and strength over longer programs, and muscle damage and power. No database search or formal selection process is described.
paper.findings: Acute studies show that protein increases myofibrillar protein synthesis after concurrent exercise compared with placebo. Over longer programs, high protein may increase lean mass, but these gains do not consistently translate into more strength, and protein at twice the recommended intake does not reverse force and power decrements.
paper.limitations: No search method is described, so study selection cannot be checked. Most trials are small and short, and few isolate the effect of protein against a resistance-only group. The author notes that running, a common aerobic mode in team sports, has been little studied with protein.
paper.practicalImplications: Athletes doing high-volume concurrent training may gain lean mass from protein above standard intakes, especially in contact sports and pre-season blocks. Protein alone is unlikely to offset strength or power losses, so the review points to recovery time between sessions and power-based training as more important levers.
paper.athleteDev: Protein above standard intakes may add lean mass for team-sport athletes doing concurrent training, but it does not add strength or power beyond that. Plan recovery time between endurance and resistance sessions and keep power-based work in the program.
paper.rtp: The review concerns training adaptation in trained adults, not recovery from injury, so it cannot guide protein or training decisions in return to sport. Its muscle damage evidence is equivocal and does not support protein for faster return after injury.

records.sourceFile: Evidence-Based Supplements for the        Enhancement of Athletic Performance.pdf

paper.citation: Peeling P, Binnie MJ, Goods PSR, Sim M, Burke LM. Evidence-Based Supplements for the Enhancement of Athletic Performance. International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism. 2018 (ahead of print).
paper.abstract: Narrative review of performance supplements grouped by strength of evidence: established (caffeine, creatine, nitrate, beta-alanine, sodium bicarbonate), equivocal (sodium citrate, phosphate, carnitine) and developing. For each supplement it summarises the event type, proposed mechanisms and common protocols.
paper.tldr: Caffeine, creatine, nitrate, beta-alanine and sodium bicarbonate have the strongest evidence for performance benefit when used at defined doses and timings. Citrate, phosphate and carnitine remain equivocal, and the developing products need more research before they can be recommended.
paper.methods: Narrative scholarly review. No search strategy, inclusion criteria or appraisal method is described. Evidence is summarised from cited studies and earlier reviews and grouped into established, equivocal and developing categories.
paper.findings: The review describes caffeine at about 3 to 6 mg/kg taken around 60 min before exercise, creatine loading of about 20 g/day for 5 to 7 days followed by a maintenance dose, and beta-alanine at 3.2 to 6.4 g/day for at least 2 to 4 weeks as having consistent benefit in the settings cited. Sodium bicarbonate benefits are mostly seen in efforts of about 60 s, with gastrointestinal upset common. Sodium citrate, phosphate and carnitine are described as equivocal, and polyphenols and N-acetylcysteine are discussed as developing options, mainly for training support and recovery.
paper.limitations: The authors describe no search method, so the selection of studies cannot be verified and the review may favour positive findings. Several claims rest on single studies or small samples. The authors also note that sport-specific evidence is lacking for some supplements, including beta-alanine, and that nitrate evidence for exercise longer than about 40 min is limited.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff should consider only supplements with a strong evidence base, and only after checking that the product is safe, legal and free of contamination risk. Any supplement should be trialled in training before competition use, because individual responses vary. The review frames supplements as an addition to a bespoke, periodised training and nutrition program built mainly on whole foods.
paper.athleteDev: The review supports considering caffeine, creatine, nitrate, beta-alanine and sodium bicarbonate for specific performance demands, using the protocols it describes. Equivocal and developing supplements should be trialled in training first, because the evidence does not establish a performance benefit for them.
paper.rtp: The review does not address injury rehabilitation or return to sport, so it cannot guide supplement choice during or after return to play.

records.sourceFile: Evidence-based nutritional approaches to enhance exercise adaptations.pdf

paper.citation: Roberts MD, Moulding B, Forbes SC, Candow DG. Evidence-based nutritional approaches to enhance exercise adaptations. Current Opinion in Clinical Nutrition and Metabolic Care. 2023;26.
paper.abstract: Opinion review of dietary supplements that support resistance training adaptations or acutely enhance strength-power or endurance performance. It covers protein, creatine monohydrate, caffeine, beetroot juice (nitrate), sodium bicarbonate and beta-alanine, with a summary table of doses and documented benefits.
paper.tldr: Protein, creatine and caffeine have the strongest support for strength, muscle and power outcomes, and caffeine, nitrate, sodium bicarbonate and beta-alanine have the most support for endurance and high-intensity efforts. Most of the evidence comes from male, non-competitive athletes over 6 to 12 weeks, so staff should adapt these protocols with care.
paper.methods: Opinion review. No search strategy, inclusion criteria or appraisal method is described. The authors discuss supplements they consider well documented, drawing on prior meta-analyses, reviews and position stands, and summarise doses in a table.
paper.findings: The authors state that protein intakes above the recommended 0.8 g/kg/day, with animal-based protein favoured, optimise muscle mass gains during resistance training, and that resistance-trained men may need more than 2.0 g/kg/day. Creatine monohydrate (20 g/day for 5 to 7 days, or 3 to 5 g/day) increased lean tissue by 1.1 kg more than placebo with resistance training in a meta-analysis of 35 trials with 1192 participants, and caffeine at 1 to 6 mg/kg taken about 60 min before exercise is described as improving strength, power and endurance (9 to 11 mg/kg may be ergolytic). For endurance and high-intensity work, the authors describe beetroot juice (6 to 8 mmol nitrate), sodium bicarbonate (about 0.3 g/kg 1 to 3 h before exercise) and beta-alanine (4 to 6 g/day for 4 weeks, with benefit possibly for efforts of 1 to 4 min) as beneficial.
paper.limitations: The authors note that most chronic supplementation studies ran for 6 to 12 weeks, that nearly all studies examined non-competitive athletes, and that most data come from male participants. They also state that beta-alanine research has mostly not shown benefit for strength or power, and that the combined effects of these supplements are untested. The review does not describe how studies were selected.
paper.practicalImplications: Protein, creatine and caffeine are the supplements the authors consider best supported for strength and power, with the doses and timing given in their table. For endurance and high-intensity work, nitrate, sodium bicarbonate and beta-alanine are the options described, with the authors noting side effects such as GI upset and paresthesia and suggesting split or multi-day dosing to reduce them. Staff should check the evidence against their own athletes' level and sex, because most of the data come from non-competitive males.
paper.athleteDev: The review supports using the listed supplements as adjuncts to training for the performance demands it describes, with the doses and timing given in its table. It does not establish benefit for competitive female athletes or for athletes at the elite level, so staff should trial protocols in training before using them in competition.
paper.rtp: The review does not address injury rehabilitation or return to sport. It cannot guide supplement use during or after return to play.

paper.citation: Lee JKW, Tan B, Ogden HB, Chapman S, Sawka MN. Exertional heat stroke: nutritional considerations. Exp Physiol. 2022;1-14.
paper.abstract: Narrative review of how nutrition and diet may influence exertional heat stroke (EHS) risk and pathophysiology in athletes, military personnel and workers. It covers carbohydrate, hydration, glutamine, bovine colostrum, antioxidants, probiotics and arginine as possible protective strategies, and ergogenic aids and low energy availability as possible harmful factors, with recommendations for future research.
paper.tldr: Nutrition may influence exertional heat stroke risk. Regular carbohydrate intake during exercise is the one strategy the authors judge to consistently dampen the physiological features of EHS, while other supplements have mixed or limited evidence and some ergogenic aids may add risk.
paper.methods: Narrative review with a conceptual model of the progression from exercise heat stress to EHS (Figure 1), and summary tables of protective strategies (Table 1) and ergogenic aids with possible harmful effects (Table 2). No systematic search method is described. Each nutritional factor is discussed for its effect on modifiable EHS pathways, including intestinal permeability, hydration, cellular thermotolerance and systemic inflammation.
paper.findings: In subclinical exertional-heat studies, carbohydrate at 30 to 90 g per hour during exercise favourably affected intestinal permeability, plasma cytokines and leukocyte function, but did not change the rise in core temperature, and the authors note it could also raise risk by increasing central drive. Euhydration reduced intestinal and blood-brain barrier permeability and acute kidney injury compared with dehydration in the cited studies, yet dehydration was not a contributing factor in 83% of military EHS cases. Glutamine, bovine colostrum, antioxidants, probiotics and arginine gave inconsistent or limited human results, while sodium bicarbonate, oral menthol and dietary nitrate were flagged as possible risk factors and caffeine has no evidence of directly contributing to EHS.
paper.limitations: The review notes that there is no universal definition of EHS and that the main protective candidates have not been directly tested for EHS outcomes in humans. Many protective findings come from rodent heat stroke models or subclinical exercise studies, and results for antioxidants, probiotics and colostrum are inconsistent. No search method is described, and the authors list youths, women, middle-aged and multi-ethnic populations among groups needing investigation.
paper.practicalImplications: Regular carbohydrate intake during prolonged exercise in the heat, within the 30 to 90 g per hour range cited by the authors, is the most consistently supported nutritional measure, but it may also let athletes push harder in the heat. Athletes and workers should begin exercise euhydrated, avoid drinking beyond sweat losses, and avoid alcohol beforehand, since alcohol may increase intestinal permeability and diuresis. Use caution with high-dose glutamine, large carbohydrate doses that cause gastrointestinal distress, and ergogenic aids such as sodium bicarbonate and oral menthol, which may cause dehydration or reduce thermal sensation.
paper.athleteDev: Relevant to staff who plan fueling and hydration for hot training and competition, since the carbohydrate and fluid strategies used for performance are the ones the review links to lower EHS-related strain. The review also flags sodium bicarbonate, oral menthol and nitrate as possible heat-risk factors when used in hot conditions.
paper.rtp: Not a return-to-play study, and it gives no criteria for return to activity. The review notes that EHS can have long-term sequelae and that a recent viral illness may increase susceptibility, which may be relevant to clearance decisions but has not been tested as a clearance criterion.
